articles.title: ‘Using the presidency to line his pockets’: could claims of corruption fuel backlash against Trump?
articles.summary: Experts say president is vulnerable amid discontent over rising prices – and the US public has ample cause for complaint
articles.body:
In Donald Trump's telling, he's a model of incorruptible self-sacrifice.

"I'm the only president that donated his salary," he told a group of cheering supporters at a Hispanic heritage month celebration in the White House last week, before conceding that George Washington – "a very wealthy person" – might have beaten him to the punch.

"They pay me $550,000 a year, and in my first term, I donated it," he continued. "In my second term I donated it too. I donated it to fixing the White House. I donated the salary into the White House preservation."

Trump's ethical self-depiction was undercut in startling fashion a day later when the crypto company that runs his memecoin offered "the most exclusive dinner in the world" at the president's members-only Trump National club in Washington.

"Join three legends and featured speaker Donald J Trump," gushed the invite to the 185 biggest investors in the Trump coin. The top 29 buyers were promised an invitation to an additional "VIP reception with your favourite president and one of the legends". For the top four donors, a Trump 18-karat gold watch lay in store.

The aim appeared to be to boost sales of the memecoin – called $Trump – over the next two months. Trump personally profits from the coin, and disclosures show he made about $636m from it last year.

With just over a month to go before November's midterm elections, Democrats seized on the dinner invitation as a political gift as they try to convert concerns over Trump's perceived corruption into a groundswell of outrage. They theorize it will power a "blue wave" that could enable the party to retake control of the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November.

"Donald Trump is vying to become the most corrupt person to ever walk the face of the earth," posted Chuck Schumer, the Democrats' leader in the US Senate.

With the US president's approval ratings already at record lows amid discontent over rising living costs fueled by the unpopular war with Iran, ethics experts say "unprecedented" levels of corruption engaged in by Trump, his family and close associates are sufficiently serious to make him vulnerable to a popular backlash.

The question is whether the myriad of accusations – many of them technical in nature – are straightforward enough to carry popular resonance.

The administration vigorously rejects the assertions, which a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, called "irresponsible" and likely to "reinforce the public's distrust in what they read".

"President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," he said in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest.

"The only special interest guiding President Trump's decision-making is the best interest of the American people. President Trump has taken on a broad swath of entrenched special interests: negotiating most-favored-nation pricing deals with major pharmaceutical companies, launching TrumpRx.gov to lower drug prices, ending unfair trade practices that international corporations have exploited to offshore jobs, and implementing schedule F to fire unelected bureaucrats who actively subvert a democratically-elected president's agenda.

"Through these actions, President Trump is delivering on his promise to empower the forgotten men and women of our country by finally putting their interests first."

Recent surveys, however, indicate American voters are more concerned than ever before about government corruption. A Gallup poll published in September recorded 89% of both all adults as saying the problem was widespread. Only Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria have registered higher levels of public concern in the past three years.

Analysts insist the US public has ample cause for complaint.

"We're facing an ethics crisis which starts and ends with a president who is constantly using his office to find new ways to personally profit," said Jordan Libowitz, communications vice-president with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a non-partisan watchdog.

"With a new story every day about Donald Trump using the presidency to line his pockets, it's no surprise that Americans are losing faith in their government."

Trump's own filings show he earned $2.2bn from his various business dealings in his first year back in the White House – including $1.4bn from his family's cryptocurrency enterprise, World Liberty Financial.

Observers identify at least three main areas of potential abuse; crypto, a venture which Trump denounced as a "fraud" just five years ago; stock trading by government officials, including the president himself; and the predictions markets, represented by companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket, both of which have links to Donald Trump Jr, and which have raised concerns about well-connected figures profiting through putting bets on government decisions and the content of official speeches.

There are also concerns about the growth of "pay to play" practices that have seen wealthy donors being granted special access and favorable decisions, including dropped criminal investigations, in exchange for donations to Trump's campaign and political Super Pac.

Presidential pardons and sentence commutations have been doled out to those who have contributed to the president's re-election effort.

As Schumer's post indicates, Democrats have increasingly tried to make corruption a campaign issue. A 30-second advertisement from Chris Pappas , a New Hampshire representative running for re-election, reflects a more widespread mood in favor of putting it center stage.

The question is whether the message on rampant graft is cutting through with an electorate that may find inflation and higher living costs easier issues to grapple with.

Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette , director of government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight , another watchdog group, acknowledged that many voters were confused by the complexity of the accusations leveled at Trump.

"Support for the Trump administration and for President Trump himself is declining pretty rapidly," he said. "But it's hard to disentangle. Is it about the corruption? Or is it about the affordability crisis continuing and in some ways getting worse?

"Corruption tends to be in the eye of the beholder. And if you ask different people about the word corruption, they say, 'Yeah, it's a problem.' But if you ask them to define what they mean by corruption, it can diverge wildly depending on how they affiliate and how they identify in terms of their partisanship and their political identity."

Brendan Fischer , director of strategic investigation at the Campaign Legal Center , said the public had been overwhelmed and "numbed" by a "fire hose" of corruption emanating from Trump's second presidency which, experts agree, has greatly exceeded that of his first administration.

"It can become overwhelming trying to keep up with each of the latest examples," said Fischer.

"I think the Trump's crypto dealings are incredibly concerning. His investments in the crypto industry open up new avenues for wealthy special interests to channel money to the president. But It's potentially harder for the public to grasp. So it hasn't broken through in the way that it that it probably should."

Easier to grasp, he believed, was Trump's acceptance of a $400m plane from Qatar , which the president has said he will use in place of the existing Air Force One.

The scale and brazenness of Trump's cavalier disregard for ethical considerations creates a danger of apathy among voters, who may feel they are powerless to change the situation as they grapple with more quotidian cost issues.

"It's easy to just throw your hands up and say, 'Everybody's corrupt, nobody's representing my interests, and my life is just not getting any better,'" Fischer said. "That is a dangerous situation for democracy. We need voters to cast their ballots and then remain engaged in the political process to make sure our elected officials are representing the interests of voters and not just their own or the interests of their donors."

Richard Painter , a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, said Trump's decision to go war with Iran opened up further corruption avenues – citing reports that both Donald Trump Jr and his brother, Eric Trump , have invested in drone manufacturers that have secured government contracts.

"Whenever there's a war, there's an enormous amount of money to be made. People say there are those who die in a war, and those who become millionaires, or maybe in this case billionaires," said Painter, now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota.

"This is what President Eisenhower talked about with the military-industrial complex back in 1961, but we've never had a president whose family actually made money from the military-industrial complex."

Painter predicted that conditions were ripe for "an enormous public backlash" but said the Democrats had to adopt a credible anti-corruption message after losing the public's confidence by failing to speak out against Hunter Biden's attempts to leverage his White House access when his father Joe Biden was president.

"The Democrats had their chance in 2021 when Biden took office, when we should have had our reawakening on ethics, and they failed," he said. "If they want to win races not only in 2026, but in 2028, they'd better get their act together and focus on ethics."

One historical model, Painter suggested, was the anti-corruption crusade championed by Jimmy Carter in his successful 1976 presidential campaign, which took place amid lingering anger at Richard Nixon over the Watergate scandal that drove him from office and his failure to quickly end the war in Vietnam.

Democrats have invoked a more recent inspiration: Hungary's recently elected prime minister, Peter Magyar, who mobilized rising resentment over government corruption in April this year to unseat the incumbent, Viktor Orbán – a close ally of Trump – in an election landslide .

Steven Levitsky, a political scientist at Harvard University and co-author, with Daniel Ziblatt, of How Democracies Die, said the key similarity between the US and Hungarian circumstances was the sense of corruption further undermining an already failing government.

"Orbán was successful in part because the economy was pretty good for much of his period in office," Levitsky said. "But eventually it slowed down, and corruption became a major factor.

"It's sad but true that in many, many cases in democracies around the world, if incumbents are perceived to be delivering – if the economy is going well, if they brought down inflation, etc – voters will turn a blind eye to corruption. It's only when you combine poor performance with corruption that it becomes salient.

"Unfortunately, in the United States, one of the things that's benefited Trump is the perception that all of politics is corrupt, mainly because of the extraordinarily outsized role of money in politics.

"There are a lot of reasons why Trump is unpopular now. Corruption is one of them but I don't think it's the principal one."

articles.title: Blue states set to trigger fresh minimum wage hikes with pay floors more than double federal rate
articles.summary: Deep-blue Washington pushes its nation-leading minimum wage to $17.73 as Seattle hits $22.14, sparking debate over labor costs and job losses.
articles.body: Workers across several Democratic-led states are set to ring in 2027 with another pay bump, widening an already sizable gap between state minimum wages and the federal floor of $7.25 an hour. Washington, California and Connecticut will all raise minimum wages that already top $17 an hour beginning Jan. 1, while New Jersey and Michigan will also hike their wage floors — widening the gap with the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour. Washington will lead the pack at $17.73 an hour, up 60 cents from its current $17.13 rate. Connecticut’s minimum wage will rise from $16.94 to $17.48, while California’s will climb from $16.90 to $17.40. New Jersey will increase its minimum wage by 56 cents to $16.48 an hour for most workers, while Michigan is slated for one of the largest jumps, rising from $13.73 to $15 an hour. AOC-BACKED $30 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN COULD BACKFIRE IN UNEXPECTED WAYS, EXPERTS WARN The hikes come as several Republican-led states have also pushed their wage floors well above the federal rate, though they remain below the highest-paying blue states. Florida’s minimum wage reached $15 an hour on Sept. 30 and will remain there through the end of 2027, while Missouri is also at $15. Nebraska will increase its minimum wage from $15 to $15.26 on Jan. 1. Washington’s statewide increase will come as Seattle pushes its own wage floor even higher. The city’s minimum wage is slated to rise to $22.14 an hour in 2027, nearly $4.50 above the new statewide rate. Seattle’s wage requirements have also become a flashpoint in the debate over the costs facing local businesses. Beginning in 2025, all employers in the city, including small businesses, became subject to the same inflation-adjusted minimum wage. Some restaurant owners who later closed their businesses cited rising labor costs among the financial pressures they faced. ECONOMIST WARNS THOUSANDS OF VIRGINIA JOBS AT RISK AFTER MINIMUM WAGE HIKE SIGNED BY SPANBERGER Washington’s minimum wage is tied to inflation under state law, with the wage floor recalculated each year rather than requiring lawmakers to approve a new increase. Washington voters approved a measure in 1998 that raised the minimum wage and, beginning in 2001, tied future increases to inflation. Voters approved another measure in 2016 that set wage increases through 2020. Since 2021, the minimum wage has again risen annually with inflation, with the goal of keeping workers’ pay in step with rising prices. Each September, the Washington Department of Labor & Industries calculates the following year’s rate based on changes in the CPI-W. The new rate is announced Sept. 30 and takes effect Jan. 1. "Democrats appear to be doing everything they can to make the business climate in Washington more untenable," Seattle Red host and conservative commentator Jason Rantz told Fox News Digital. DOWNTOWN SEATTLE LOST 30,000 JOBS, BILLIONS IN OFFICE VALUE SINCE 2020 PAYROLL TAX: NEW REPORT FINDS "It’s not just the high cost of labor — Seattle is now going to be over $22 an hour — but it’s the high crime, open-air drug use, new income tax that targets pass-through businesses, and overregulation that make operating businesses more difficult than it should be," Rantz said. "Our unemployment rate is higher than the national average, and we’re losing tech jobs left and right," he added. "Democrats have no answers. They’re just making their problems worse." The wage hike comes as Washington’s unemployment rate reached 4.9% in August, above the 4.1% national rate and up from 4.6% a year earlier, according to the state Employment Security Department. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Washington also lost an estimated 900 jobs that month, including 2,300 information-sector positions, while professional and business services employment was down 13,100 jobs from a year earlier. Angela Rosen, who founded Penelope and the Beauty Bar and operates three Seattle spas, told Rantz that her therapists already make more than minimum wage, but said higher labor costs have squeezed support positions instead. "I had to cut my front desk," Rosen told "The Jason Rantz Show," according to Seattle Red. Rantz reported that the move eliminated 12 shifts per week across two smaller locations.

articles.title: Battle over daylight saving time erupts as push to stop changing clocks hits Senate wall
articles.summary: President Donald Trump shared Tom Cotton's phone number to pressure the senator on the "Sunshine Protection Act," but Cotton warns of dark winter mornings.
articles.body: The battle over Americans’ clocks reemerged in an unlikely way over the weekend, with President Donald Trump picking a fight with one of his top allies over the issue. There have been many fights in Congress over the nearly two years that Trump has been in office for his second term that either ended in partisan victory or gloriously fizzled out, but one has quietly gone onto the shelf despite his pressure on Republicans to do something about it. And that fight is over allowing states to voluntarily observe daylight saving time year-round to effectively do away with the twice-a-year ritual of changing clocks. It’s a popular issue with voters and the president, and there’s a bill that passed the House this summer to enact the change. But it’s a policy issue that has divided both sides of the aisle and ground to a halt in the upper chamber. TRUMP URGES SENATE TO PASS BILL MAKING DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME PERMANENT AFTER OVERWHELMING HOUSE VOTE Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., has been one of the more vocal opponents of the bill, vowing to block any attempts to fast-track it on the floor. That resistance earned him a Truth Social post from Trump, who over the weekend shared his personal phone number in a bid to pressure the lawmaker to change his stance on daylight saving time. "Almost everybody wants "The Sunshine Protection Act" to pass, except for Tom Cotton," Trump said. "To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself." Cotton responded, noting that Congress has tackled daylight saving time before, only to roll back the change shortly after. "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first." TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END In the 1970s, lawmakers did enact year-round daylight saving time. But Americans rapidly soured on the change, especially parents whose children had to wait in the dark for the school bus. It was repealed about a year later. And Cotton recently answered an off-the-cuff question from a fellow Republican during their weekly closed-door policy lunches, a source told Fox News Digital, where he made a similar case as his response to Trump. No one pushed back during the meeting. The issue of daylight saving time, and supporting a permanent fix or sticking to the status quo are more geographical than political. It’s, in part, mountainous and Western states versus coastal states. On one side of the spectrum are lawmakers like Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and Patty Murray, D-Wash., who introduced a Senate version of the bill last year. "Every year, more Americans grow more frustrated setting their clocks back and forth, and every winter folks in Washington state despair at the prospect of losing an hour of precious sunlight when we are forced off Daylight Saving Time," Murray said in a statement at the time. HOUSE PASSES DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME REFORM AS TRUMP SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR ENDING CLOCK CHANGE Lawmakers in landlocked states out West, like Sens. Steve Daines, R-Mont., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warn that it would cause kids in their states to go to school in the dark. "I can see where Florida likes it for tee times at certain times of the year, but it doesn’t work so well for moms and dads putting kids on buses when the sunrise in Western Montana wouldn’t be till 9:30 in the morning. It’s not going to work for us," Daines told CNN in July. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The most vital currency in the Senate is floor time. And lawmakers won’t have much floor time to spare when they return after the midterm elections in November. Though it’s popular, more pressing issues like the National Defense Authorization Act, supplemental funding for the war and a looming government funding battle will likely take precedence. And Republican leaders acknowledge that it’s not as easy as a simple yes-or-no vote for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. "Depends where you're living in the country and the impact — what it would be, in your own home state," Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said in July. "So it's not as simple as what one state might like."

articles.title: Alito says Supreme Court can’t stem emergency appeals and voices concern over Trump’s rhetoric
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says the escalating volume of emergency appeals before the court isn't a good thing, but he adds there's...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito says the escalating volume of emergency appeals before the court isn't a good thing, but he adds there's little the court can do to change the trajectory.

The number of petitions asking the justices to intervene quickly has skyrocketed during President Donald Trump's second administration, putting the court at the center of hotly debated issues such as the Republican president's new ballroom construction and his proposed restrictions on mail ballots in the midterm elections.

The number of emergency applications now rivals the annual tally of cases the justices consider with full briefing and oral arguments, Alito wrote in a new book released Tuesday.

The justice told The Associated Press in a rare interview that the rhetoric about the court from Trump and his administration doesn't sit well with him.

"I personally am not pleased with that," he said. "Everybody in this country has the right to criticize what we do. The substance of their criticism can be quite harsh. If we deserve it, then that's fine. But rhetoric is a different story."

Alito spoke in connection with his first book, "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of The Constitution, The Court and Our Country."

Coming 20 years after he was confirmed to the court after his nomination by President George W. Bush, a Republican, the book is a collection of speeches the 76-year-old has given over the years on religious liberty, his judicial philosophy and constitutional rights.

Alito calls it 'offensive' to cast his opinions as MAGA

Alito is perhaps best known for writing the decision that reversed Roe v. Wade and ended abortion as a nationwide right, and he has been one of the most consistent members of the court's conservative bloc. He's also voted in favor of some of Trump's signature policies, even those the rest of the conservative wing has struck down. But he rejects the idea that his decisions are in the "Make America Great Again" camp.

"It's offensive," he said. "I honestly try to decide every single case on the merits, every single application on the merit. And that's true whether the president is Donald Trump or Joe Biden or Barack Obama or anybody else."

Trump, for his part, has cheered Alito as "one of the Greatest of All Time" even as he maligned justices whom he appointed as "unpatriotic" and "merely a shell of their original selves." Alito said the harsh rhetoric from across the spectrum doesn't affect how the justices rule but does play a role in the public's declining trust in the court.

"The terms used by presidents and by members of their administration, Cabinet officers, other high-ranking officers in describing the Supreme Court and their decisions, and sometimes individual justices, is far different from what we saw 15 years ago," Alito said.

Much of the president's frustration has come after the court ruled against him on some of his central initiatives, including tariffs and birthright citizenship . Those decisions have been handed down after months of consideration, including oral arguments.

Surge in court's emergency decisions is likely 'going to continue'

In emergency decisions, by contrast, the president has a much stronger track record of wins.

Typically made in days or weeks, emergency orders are designed to be temporary, lasting only as cases continue to play out in lower courts. But since that process can take years, those decisions can still have important real-world consequences.

Critics, including Alito's liberal-leaning colleague Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson , have complained about the court's recent handling of the emergency docket and outlined proposed steps the justices could take.

Alito, though, said there's little the court can do to stem the tide. Presidents have increasingly used executive orders to enact their policies rather than passing laws through Congress, leading to lawsuits and "robust" decisions from lower-court judges that send a case quickly to the Supreme Court, he said.

"Unless something changes there, and I don't foresee it right now, I'm afraid this is going to continue," he said. "An application is something that I think we have to rule on."

Alito says recusal from climate change case wasn't required but a 'judgment call'

Alito also detailed his decision to step away from hearing a climate change case that opened the term . Dozens of similar lawsuits have been filed on whether cities can sue oil and gas companies over damage linked to global warming. Billions of dollars could be at stake, a potentially serious threat to the industry, according to court documents.

Alito had faced calls to recuse himself because he owns stock in oil companies. He told the AP that the stock came from an inheritance his wife received from her father that she doesn't want to sell.

He initially stayed on the case because he doesn't have stock in the companies involved, he said, adding that the court's legal office agreed that he could hear the case under its ethics code .

But as he delved deeper into the substance of the case, he decided to step aside.

"This particular decision was a judgment call," he said. "I gave it very, very serious consideration."

articles.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom called the remarks "deranged", but the White House said Trump was warning of the risk of a nuclear Iran.
articles.body:
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.

California Governor Gavin Newsom responded to the comments - made by Trump during a midterms rally in Nebraska - as "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".

According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.

Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.

While speaking in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, he said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."

There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".

In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was "disgusting and disqualifying".

Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.

In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".

"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".

The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.

A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.

"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance," the account added.

San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.

It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.

Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.

It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.

This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.

articles.title: Two key groups launch Latino voter turnout operation in South Texas
articles.summary: The Voto Latino Foundation and the Hispanic Federation are spending six figures to get voters to the polls in the Rio Grande Valley.
articles.body: Latino voters are upset about the cost of living and immigration enforcement operations, according to polls and interviews. Whether they actually show up to vote in November — and in what numbers — is another question. Getting Latinos to the polls next month is a central push of two of the largest Latino advocacy organizations in the country, the Voto Latino Foundation and the Hispanic Federation, according to plans first shared with NBC News. This week, the groups are launching a six-figure get-out-the-vote operation that specifically targets Texas’ Rio Grande Valley, where they estimate that nearly 316,000 Latinos who could vote did not participate in the 2024 election. In 2024, Latino voters in the Valley made history when a majority backed Donald Trump. Since then, many key figures have come out opposing Trump’s policies, including his economic plans and how the administration is carrying out deportations. In addition to those who sat out in 2024, the advocacy groups say nearly 500,000 Texas Latinos have turned 18 in the last two years and are now eligible to vote. On Saturday, the groups will host a community town hall in Edinburg called “Juntos en el 956,” where organizers will assist residents with making plans to vote and answer questions. Claudia Lopez, a social media personality in the Rio Grande Valley who focuses on South Texas politics, will moderate the town hall. Another televised town hall will follow in cooperation with Telemundo, and an end-of-the-month rally to promote voter turnout is in the works. Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of the Hispanic Federation, said he believes educating Latinos about their voting rights and hearing their concerns is central to improving turnout. “When we do this right, we are going to see a correlation in the participation of Latinos on Election Day,” Miranda said. Talking to voters, he said, the group will encourage people to vote early and, for those already registered to vote, to check ahead of time that nothing happened with their registrations. “In many places, there have been attempts to try to push people out of the voter rolls, to try to question some of the data,” he said. “We want to make sure that people are prepared, that people know exactly what to do when they get to the polls, whether their name is there or their name is not there.” María Teresa Kumar, president and co-founder of the Voto Latino Foundation, said part of its job is to make sure people understand the electoral significance of the Valley. “It is going to be the epicenter of the Latino vote for the rest of the country. If the Latino vote in this area swings drastically back to the Democratic side, not only is it going to be indicative of where the Latino vote is today, but it is going to be the beginning of a building block of what people can expect in ’28,” she said. “Our focus is to get people really informed, making sure that they turn out.” An NBC News/Telemundo survey of 800 registered Latino voters nationally showed Trump with 69% disapproval among respondents, and 54% said they intended their midterm votes to signal opposition to him. Latinos in Texas, however, are historically underrepresented at the polls. Kumar said that among the messages to voters is to vote early. “It inoculates you; it’s hard for people to say anybody cheated, but No. 2, it also gives people the courage to go ahead and vote, too, because they see their neighbors doing it,” she said.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: The biggest surprises come after October
articles.summary: Democrats play defense in Minnesota and New Hampshire while Republicans spend big in Arkansas, Mississippi, and Idaho ahead of the midterms.
articles.body: Four weeks out from the election, and for most Americans, it’s time for football, foliage and flannel. For politics watchers, all eyes are on an October surprise. They’ve been game-changers before. In 2008, the collapse of Lehman Brothers, which ushered in the biggest financial crisis since the Great Depression, was a turning point in John McCain’s presidential campaign. He was even with Barack Obama when the news broke, then trailed in every survey after. He lost the popular vote by seven points. Surprises have come from home and abroad. In 1980, it was President Jimmy Carter’s inability to resolve the Iranian hostage crisis. Eight years earlier, it was President Richard Nixon’s announcement that "peace was at hand" in Vietnam. Some have more impact than others. It’s not clear that news about George W. Bush’s DUI changed much about the 2000 election, nor that James Comey’s letter to Congress about Hillary Clinton’s email server was the decider in President Trump’s 2016 win. Still, these surprises all have one thing in common: they happened in presidential years. EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS, TOP REPUBLICAN PREDICTS: ‘YOU’RE GONNA SEE SURPRISES’ It’s not as though we don’t get breaking news during the last month of a midterm cycle. Take 2018, when the GOP warned about a migrant caravan, Brett Kavanaugh sought a seat on the Supreme Court, and a gunman opened fire at a Pittsburgh synagogue. But that was the exception, not the rule. For the most part, midterm October surprises affect individual races, not the overall trajectory of a party. In the last midterm, for example, Herschel Walker faced damaging allegations about paying for former girlfriends’ abortions, while in Florida, the destruction caused by Hurricane Ian gave Gov. Ron DeSantis the opportunity to show Floridians that he could be trusted to handle a crisis. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? Voters haven’t changed their minds about Trump or the party they’d prefer to elect to the House for several months now, so local stories like these are the ones to watch in the final weeks of the campaign. Besides, the biggest surprises come after October. Democrats are playing more defense than they’d like For what still looks like a good – maybe great – year for the Democrats, the party is playing defense in some unexpected places. DAVID MARCUS: IN DEEP BLUE MINNESOTA A RED DAWN MAY BE RISING AHEAD OF THE MIDTERMS That starts with Minnesota, where Republicans have a star candidate in Michele Tafoya. The former NFL sideline reporter has been up and down the state with a message to "stop the fraud" if elected to the Senate. That’s been a hot issue in the state, and it’s allowed her to target the Democrat, Peggy Flanagan, who currently serves as lieutenant governor. Then there’s New Hampshire, another state where Democrats are in the driver’s seat thanks to this political environment, but where the GOP has a favorable match up. Former U.S. Senator John E. Sununu is back on the ballot this year against Chris Pappas, who seems to have had trouble animating his voters. Even Oregon’s gubernatorial race is competitive this year. Solid Republican states could have closer-than-expected margins Meanwhile, Republicans are spending money in surprising places. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. In Arkansas, Sen. Tom Cotton has thrown $13.6 million at his reelection bid, outspending his Democratic opponent Hallie Schoffner 65 to 1. Cotton may have ambitions beyond his current role in the Senate, but in 2020, his spending fell short of $1 million. Idahoans got a letter in the mail from Vice President Vance last month warning them that Democrats could "pour millions of dollars" into independent challenger Todd Achilles; Vance called it an "urgent national race." Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has been running ads attacking her Democratic challenger Scott Colom in recent weeks, calling him a "failed prosecutor" with a "chilling" record on crime; that state has seen $5 million in ad spending so far this year. FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON And Florida is full of election surprises. In 2018, Rick Scott won his Senate race by 0.1 percentage points while DeSantis won his by 0.4 points. Two years later, the presidential race was decided by just 3.4 points. Nebraska and South Dakota could be closer-than-expected for Republicans as well. In this week’s Power Rankings, one Carolina gets more competitive while another drifts away from the GOP, and Democrats get nervous about a governor’s race in Oregon. Senate: Shifts in North and South Carolina make it eight battlegrounds The math is the same in the Senate. Each party has 47 seats to their name, leaving six toss-up races to determine control. Those are Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas, which all look close in the flurry of surveys released by pollsters last week. Two other races are highly competitive: New Hampshire (Lean D) and Kansas (Lean R). On the polling alone, these look more like toss-up states: surveys released last week have the Democrat ahead by only five points in New Hampshire, and the Kansas race dead even. It’s the partisan makeup of these states that keeps them at "lean." North Carolina is less competitive than it was two weeks ago. Fox News confirmed on Friday that the Senate Leadership Fund, a powerful Super PAC aligned with Republican leadership, was pulling resources from the state. Earlier, Sen. Tim Scott left it off a list of states where Republicans were focusing spending. GOP nominee Michael Whatley is running as strong a race as he can there, and the margin will probably be tighter than polls currently have it. But the Democrat, Roy Cooper, is also a strong candidate, and he has had double-digit leads in multiple surveys. North Carolina moves from Lean D to Likely D. Nearby South Carolina is getting more competitive. Darline Graham, appointed to the Senate after the death of her brother, Lindsey, is reportedly getting more help on the campaign trail from President Trump. There are lingering questions about Graham’s ability to turn out a broad spectrum of Republican voters against a Democratic candidate who, like her counterparts in Kansas and Nebraska, is pushing hard on the price of diesel. The state moves from Solid R to Likely R. Governor: Oregon is a battleground; keep an eye on Florida and Vermont Four years ago, Oregonians sent Tina Kotek to the governor’s mansion for the first time, and it hasn’t gone smoothly. Kotek faces four issues all at once in this campaign, as outlined in local reports and on the trail: a housing crisis, poor education outcomes, higher city crime rates than in neighboring states, and like other incumbents, she flip-flopped on data centers. A lethargic debate performance last week didn’t help matters. Drazan has lost this race before, and this time, won’t get help from a third-party candidate who drew votes from the Democrat. But this time around, she has created more distance both from Trump and conversations about abortion, which she calls a "settled issue." Democrats have every reason to hold on to this state in November, but it’s going to be tougher than the party wants. Oregon moves from Likely D to Lean D. Elsewhere, two states are becoming more competitive for Democrats, beginning with Florida. The Sunshine State is the home of the "MAGA" movement, and Rep. Byron Donalds easily locked up the Republican nomination in August. But he has stumbled, at times, on the campaign trail, and Hispanic voters continue to express frustration with this economy. Florida moves from Solid R to Likely R. And in Vermont, longtime incumbent Republican Phil Scott might have raised an eyebrow at a new poll from the University of New Hampshire showing his Democratic opponent, Amanda Janoo, up six points against Scott, 49% to 43%. The Green Mountain State also moves from Solid R to Likely R.

articles.title: Millions saved by blocking dead people payouts as Trump Treasury drops hammer on federal fraud
articles.summary: Treasury's "Do Not Pay" program screened over 1.1 billion payments worth $3.7 trillion, catching 13,500 improper payments to deceased people.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Treasury Department blocked $175 million in federal payments tied to deceased recipients in fiscal year 2026, up sharply from the $99 million identified just months earlier as the Trump administration expanded government-wide screening for improper payments. "I applaud Secretary [Scott] Bessent for slamming the door on these fraudsters before they can pick taxpayers’ pockets," Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Fox News Digital. "Unless you were playing Frisbee in the quad during Econ 101, you know the federal government shouldn’t be sending taxpayer money to dead people," Kennedy went on. "I fought for years to pass my common-sense bill to stop fraudsters from gaming the system, and now it’s the law." Kennedy has for years pushed to give Treasury greater access to Social Security death records, helping pass a 2020 law that temporarily authorized the Social Security Administration to share its full Death Master File with the department. That three-year data-sharing program began in December 2023. Trump then signed Kennedy’s Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act into law in February 2026, making access permanent. TRUMP'S WAR ON FRAUD EXPANDS AS TREASURY LAUNCHES NEW SITE WITH WHISTLEBLOWER INCENTIVES Trump has tasked his administration with rooting out fraud, waste and abuse across the federal government and tightening safeguards around taxpayer dollars — the latest effort to stop federal benefit payments to dead people is just another initiative within that broader effort. "President Trump continues to deliver for Americans where previous administrations have fallen short. This Administration is setting new standards in record time to prevent fraud and improper payments before hard-earned taxpayer dollars leave the Treasury. Under President Trump’s leadership, there is no tolerance for waste, fraud, and abuse," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. Treasury screened more than 1.1 billion federal payments totaling roughly $3.7 trillion in FY2026, identifying and returning about 13,500 payments worth $175 million that otherwise would have been distributed to individuals no longer eligible for payments due to death. "Treasury continues to transform how the federal government protects taxpayer dollars by using better data, stronger controls, and advanced technology to stop fraud and improper payments before money goes out the door," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release shared with Fox News Digital. "In the past year alone, Treasury built and deployed new safeguards that verified more than $3.7 trillion in federal payments and increased Do Not Pay access from 4 percent of programs to 99 percent, ensuring agencies have access to the data they need," Bessent added. "We are moving beyond ‘pay and chase’ and making prevention the federal government’s first line of defense." WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE More than 99% of federal programs now have access to the "Do Not Pay" tool, up from roughly 4% at the end of FY2025. The expansion fulfills key requirements of a March 2025 executive order from Trump directing his administration to strengthen safeguards against fraud, waste and abuse involving federal payments. Treasury also screened more than 2.3 billion records against Do Not Pay data sources in FY2026, nearly four times the 641 million records screened the previous fiscal year. The jump comes as the program has expanded across the federal government, alongside new payment verification efforts and additional screenings for states. VANCE TO HOST CONGRESS AT WHITE HOUSE TO DISCUSS LEGISLATIVE ACTION ON FRAUD Treasury also tested new safeguards aimed at verifying that bank accounts belong to the intended recipients and checking Taxpayer Identification Numbers tied to federal payments. The checks became fully operational Sept. 30 and allow Treasury to flag and return payments that fail verification before the money is sent. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest figures build on Treasury’s July announcement that it had screened more than 885 million payments worth roughly $2.77 trillion and flagged more than 4,900 payments worth about $99 million tied to deceased recipients.

articles.title: NYT columnist thrashed online for suggesting Trump is to blame for alleged Cornell gang rape
articles.summary: New York Times columnist Michelle Cottle blamed Trump for the culture behind an alleged Cornell University gang rape that occurred under Biden.
articles.body: The New York Times is under fire after one of its columnists suggested that President Donald Trump is responsible for creating the culture that led to an alleged sexual assault against a woman at Cornell University by seven men. "What this is, is it's a fundamental disrespect for women," columnist Michelle Cottle said on ABC News on Sunday. "You can't send those messages no matter how drunk you are as a frat boy without having some kind of misunderstanding about what women are there for and whether this is a real person you're dealing with." "And that, I think, starts, you know — we can go to the president for this one," Cottle went on. "I mean, we are in a moment in this culture where the glorification of being thuggish and swaggering and mistreating women is kind of making you a cool kid." CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS A woman identified as Jane Doe in court records has filed a civil lawsuit against seven men she alleges gang-raped her during a ketamine- and alcohol-induced incident at Cornell University in 2024. Former President Joe Biden occupied the White House at that time. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some saying the sex was consensual, and others saying they didn't participate. No charges have been filed. AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS The backlash to Cottle's comments was fierce, especially among those pointing out that the incident happened when Biden was president, including Fox News contributor Joe Concha. "This happened in 2024 when Biden was President. Did she not know that?" another X user asked. "Latest edition of 'Trump turned me into a newt!' brought to you by a very very smart person," said CNN contributor Scott Jennings. "Media and pundits fall all over themselves trying to make everything and anything about Donald Trump. It’s embarrassing and so incredibly lazy," said Tricia McLaughlin, former assistant secretary for public affairs at the Department of Homeland Security. "This take is SO far beyond delusional that you can’t even see sanity from here…" said conservative commentator John Ziegler. "Of course, it's Trump's fault," said the Media Research Center, which first posted the clip. ATTORNEY FOR ACCUSED CORNELL STUDENT CALLS ON LETITIA JAMES TO STEP ASIDE OVER PRIOR COMMENTS Trump has commented on the case, which is now being investigated by longtime foe New York Attorney General Letitia James, who in 2022 filed a civil fraud lawsuit against him. Trump in 2024 was found liable for fraud and ordered to pay more than $350 million, but the penalty was overturned on appeal. Asked about James being appointed to investigate the alleged gang rape, Trump launched into an attack on the state attorney general. "Well, Letitia James is a corrupt person," Trump said. "She's totally corrupt, and I can't imagine it — I feel badly for whoever she's looking at because they won't get a fair shake. Letitia James is a corrupt person." articles.title: Newsom tags in State Threat Assessment Center over Trump’s Iran nuclear comments
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Tuesday said he directed the State Threat Assessment Center to monitor for any possible threats to the Golden State after President Trump’s “invitation” for Iran to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. “Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous — if not treasonous — putting a target on two of…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Tuesday said he directed the State Threat Assessment Center to monitor for any possible threats to the Golden State after President Trump’s “invitation” for Iran to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

“Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous — if not treasonous — putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom wrote on the social platform X . “I am directing the State Threat Assessment Center to actively monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California.”

Newsom and other officials from the state blasted the president for remarks he made during a rally in Grand Island, Neb., on Monday. Trump was defending his administration’s conflict with Iran when he suggested that if Tehran could “take out” the two southern California cities, it would be “a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

White House communications director Steven Cheung claimed shortly after that Trump “was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped” and accused the backlash of being a “media freakout.”

The White House’s Rapid Response X account also clapped back at the Los Angeles Times’s report that quoted the president, calling the outlet “buffoons.”

Newsom, who is weighing a 2028 presidential run , called Trump “deranged and dangerous” for making such a suggestion. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) and San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) also lambasted Trump.

“San Diego is not collateral damage,” Gloria wrote on the social platform X . “We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

At least one San Diego Republican, House candidate and former San Marcos, Calif., Mayor Jim Desmond, said on the social platform X that he served in the U.S. Navy to protect his countrymen, “not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war.”

“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments,” Desmond continued. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland … No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Bass has fought off suggestions made by the president to use the City of Angels as a battleground, including his notion of using Democratic-led cities as “training grounds’ for U.S. service members. The mayor accused Trump in October 2025 of wanting to use the military “against the American people.”

“You are talking about creating warfare within cities, and again, I will point out, there’s something these cities have in common,” she told CNN last year, referring to the city’s Democratic hierarchy.

articles.title: With SAVE Act fail, Republicans snatch failure from the jaws of success
articles.summary: Republican leadership never identified what sort of compromise could earn 60 votes
articles.body:
The SAVE Act should have been the easiest layup for Republican leaders. Instead, they dribbled out the clock, argued with the referees and then congratulated themselves for preserving the rules of their political game at the expense of the American people.

Public agreement on voter ID was hardly ambiguous. An August 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 83 percent of U.S. adults favored government-issued photo identification to vote, including 95 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents and 71 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. That represents agreement on a principle — not a blanket endorsement of the later SAVE America Act.

The House passed the SAVE Act in July 2024 and April 2025. Neither effort became law. On February 11, 2026, it passed the expanded SAVE America Act, 218–213, combining documentary proof of citizenship for federal voter registration with photo identification for voting and other election provisions. On March 26, Senate cloture on a narrower photo-ID amendment drew 53 votes. An August 8 vote to advance a stand-alone photo-ID bill drew 52. Both fell short of the 60 votes required to advance.

That is the brief procedural history, not a postmortem … yet

Four overlapping reasons explain the failure to pass legislation: substantive disagreement, partisan polarization, legislative overreach and institutional choice.

First, there were legitimate disagreements over substance that should have been apparent to congressional leaders. This was more than a command to show identification. It addressed citizenship documents, acceptable IDs, name discrepancies, federal data, voter rolls, mail voting and implementation burdens.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) supported voter ID but opposed the broader bill over federalism, rural access, document availability and implementation problems that are particularly acute in Alaska. Those concerns deserved serious answers. Those concerns should have been visible early on and not spooked the Republicans into abandoning the bill. Competent party leadership would have treated internal opposition as an invitation to negotiate

Second, partisan polarization transformed a solvable design problem into a loyalty test. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) invoked the Freedom to Vote Act, proposed in 2021 but never enacted. A floor speech, a press release, or a press conference is no substitute for putting a viable counterproposal before the Senate. That earlier bill included broader identification options and voter protections, but also redistricting and campaign-finance changes. It was a sweeping election package, hardly a narrow answer to the voter-ID dispute.

The question was how to turn the overlap into legislation. Neither party delivered that agreement.

Republicans eventually separated photo ID from the citizenship-document provisions, but no Democrat voted to advance any narrower proposal. Confusion prompts a few logical questions. First, what will it take for Democrats to accept a conciliation that they explicitly requested? Second, whom do they serve — the American people, or their own political agenda?

Both parties complicated the case. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), working with President Trump and the White House, proposed election provisions alongside restrictions on transgender participation in women’s sports and transition-related surgeries for minors. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) filed voting-related amendments alongside proposals on cryptocurrency, airline rewards and other subjects.

This was not pork in the traditional Washington sense. It was an election bill carrying unrelated policy demands. Those proposals widened the fight when Congress needed to narrow its disagreements. Only Congress could turn a political layup into a full-court shot — and then blame the basket for the miss.

Finally and most importantly, institutional choice caused this failure. The filibuster did not descend from Mount Sinai engraved on a third tablet. Against Trump’s insistence, Republicans chose to preserve it; Democrats used it to block legislation. Republican leaders could have narrowed the bill further and negotiated for votes, or pursued rules changes. Neither path guaranteed success.

Instead, Republicans let the clock run out before the August recess. They could then blame Democrats and Senate procedure for the delay. Preserving procedure took priority over passing legislation.

Democrats offered both legitimate objections and disingenuous amendments, but did little else to bridge the divide. Republicans squandered the power they had from controlling both chambers of Congress. The culpability scale therefore tips to the Republicans: “with power, comes great responsibility.”

The deepest failure is that Republican leadership never identified what sort of compromise could earn 60 votes. The public record is crowded with speeches, amendments, procedural maneuvers and accusations. It is remarkably thin on sustained bipartisan bargaining over the practical questions that separated the parties. The Republicans produced roll-call votes and campaign talking points not a governing coalition.

As a result, election policy will continue to be shaped by doomed executive action, flawed federal litigation and a patchwork of state laws — approaches that can be less successful, uniform and durable than federal legislation.

The Republican Leadership’s failure to resolve the dispute within its caucus is inexcusable and telling. Either Senate Republican Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) does not possess an intelligible playbook or he received orders not to act. Should Democrats win control of either chamber in November, as polling indicates they will, the SAVE America Act will likely be dead. We should reject excuses and encourage lawmakers to resolve their political differences and legislate — not to manufacture new conflicts, leaving the American people to once again bear the consequences.

Donald J. Slaughter Sr. is a publisher and media executive.

articles.title: Trump won’t reimburse government for controversial ads

articles.body:
The White House clarified Tuesday that President Trump will not pay back the federal government for money already spent on controversial political TV ads after he said he would start paying for the ads himself.

Trump said Monday he would pay for the controversial “Patriotic Ads” himself after receiving backlash for using taxpayer money to fund them.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” the president added.

But a White House official confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, that Trump does not plan to reimburse the money already spent, saying, “The President’s Truth was not referring to reimbursement.”

The ads were part of a $20 million campaign and feature Trump’s voice saying the country will defeat socialism and communism.

Democrats and some Republicans quickly criticized the ads.

The White House defended them, saying they weren’t political.

“The president is not on the ballot, and the ads don’t have a call to action,” a White House official said.

Vice President Vance defended the ads too, saying there’s precedent for the federal government to use taxpayer money to promote government actions, pointing to Obama-era ads for the Affordable Care Act.

“It’s part of, actually, I think, living in a constitutional republic,” Vance told reporters Monday. “You have to be honest with the American people about what you’re doing, about what’s going on.”

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) head Brendan Carr said there was nothing in the ads that “strikes me as out of the ordinary or that would merit any sort of FCC review.”

articles.title: Scarborough says GOP closing message ‘out of touch,’ slams Trump’s California comments
articles.summary: MS NOW host Joe Scarborough on Monday slammed Republicans’ closing message for the midterms. “I’ve got to say, across the country, you’ve got gas prices at record highs, you’ve got diesel prices at record highs. Just telling people, ‘Hey, don’t worry about it. This is just short-term pain. Don’t worry about it. It’s worth it,…
articles.body:
MS NOW host Joe Scarborough on Monday slammed Republicans’ closing message for the midterms.

“I’ve got to say, across the country, you’ve got gas prices at record highs, you’ve got diesel prices at record highs. Just telling people, ‘Hey, don’t worry about it. This is just short-term pain. Don’t worry about it. It’s worth it, it’s worth it. You know, by the way, if they do get nukes, let them annihilate Los Angeles and San Diego. But it’s worth it,’” Scarborough said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe,” referencing a comment from President Trump at a rally where he suggested Iran could “take out” two major U.S. cities in California.

“I don’t know that that’s a good closing message for a Republican Party that is faring worse in polls,” he said, citing a Gallup poll which he said showed the GOP 11 points behind Democrats.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The talk show host then pointed to Dr. Mehmet Oz’s recent Fox News appearance, where the head of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) suggested the price of butter was only $1.

Scarborough later added that “we’re seeing exactly how out of touch” Republicans “are in this final run.”

Republicans are facing an uphill battle as they head into the midterms this year, grappling with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living.

Energy costs have risen amid the war in Iran, with the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, closed amid the conflict. According to AAA , the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.37 on Tuesday afternoon and the average price of a gallon of diesel was about $6.32.

On Monday, Trump made a comment suggesting Iran could “take out” two large cities in California if the Middle Eastern country made a nuclear weapon. The president’s comment came during remarks at a political rally in Grand Island, Neb., where he defended the war against Iran despite increased prices for American consumers.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, for keeping our country safe,” Trump said, adding that Iran could “take out a city.”

“Let ‘em take out Los Angeles, let ‘em take out San Diego,” he continued. “This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that “no one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the President understands how to communicate with them.”

articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday blasted Fox News over its recent interviews with Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed (D) of Michigan and Dan Osborn (I) of Nebraska.

Trump questioned on Truth Social why the network would interview the “sleazebag, Dan Osborn right now, who is running against our GREAT Republican Senator Pete Ricketts.” He then referred to his winning Nebraska in 2016, 2020 and 2024 as a “miracle … by a landslide.”

The president also accused Fox News of covering El-Sayed more “than they do the good old fashioned Republicans, the people that have saved America, and are making it great again.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“All they talk about is Dumocrat Jihadists like El-Sayed, with his softball interview by Martha MacCallum, and the like,” Trump wrote earlier on Tuesday. “She never interviews me like that. They don’t show my record breaking Rallies the morning after, but others do, and that’s what MAGA is watching.”

The posts follow Trump’s general, lengthy complaint on Sunday that the network’s “Fox & Friends” series did not cover recent Republican rallies in Ohio, Alabama, Texas and Oklahoma. He called the rallies “the hottest things out there” but “nothing shows up on Fox!”

“Other networks are reporting about these Rallies, and really positively, like ‘crazy!'” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday . “Our people want to see our Rallies, and reports on our Rallies, on FoxNews, or they will very quickly stop watching (like I am doing right now!).”

His characterization of the network’s sitdown with El-Sayed as “softball” contrasts with Fox News’s own description of the interview .

The outlet said El-Sayed was challenged for accepting donations from wealthy donors after campaigning against corporate donors. El-Sayed told MacCallum that he welcomes support from individuals who want to contribute.

“You know what I don’t do? I don’t call corporations. I don’t call AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] … Individuals who want to support a campaign, that’s different,” he said.

Trump also lamented last Wednesday that Fox News was hosting Democrats for interviews on its network, accusing the network of giving Democrats “more airtime than Pro Republicans.”

“They repeat a completely negative narrative, on and on it goes, and then we get a quick retort. It’s truly amazing that I won all three Elections,” he wrote on Truth Social, repeating his false claim that he won the 2020 election, which he lost to former President Biden.

The president has long praised Fox News and welcomed many of the network’s former personalities into his orbit, from advisory roles to Cabinet positions in his administration. Conversely, former Trump administration officials including White House press secretaries Kayleigh McEnany and Karoline Leavitt have left to eventually land jobs at the network.

Fox News, among other major TV networks that rotate covering the president for wider media distribution, paused that coverage last month in response to Trump’s attempt to ban CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from covering the White House.

articles.title: Schumer alleges illegal coordination between Trump, PAC on ads
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is moving to investigate President Trump for allegedly misusing taxpayer dollars to pay for government-sponsored campaign ads. Schumer announced Tuesday that he is demanding that two government watchdog agencies investigate and preserve records related to the administration’s effort to make PSA television ads that portray Trump in a favorable…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is moving to investigate President Trump for allegedly misusing taxpayer dollars to pay for government-sponsored campaign ads .

Schumer announced Tuesday that he is demanding that two government watchdog agencies investigate and preserve records related to the administration’s effort to make PSA television ads that portray Trump in a favorable light and are reminiscent of Trump campaign ads.

Schumer also said he will report Trump to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) for illegal coordination with the MAGA Inc. political action committee, which Trump said will now start paying for the ads. Federal officeholders are by law prohibited from coordinating with super PACs like MAGA Inc.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The $20 million ad campaign has been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. The series of ads that have run so far contain the disclaimer “Paid by the U.S. Government” and the funds originally came out of money intended for the Department of Homeland Security, according to a report from The New York Times .

Schumer, in a press release announcing the moves, called the ads “propaganda.”

“Trump has gutted funding for health care and other essential programs but he nonetheless found millions of dollars — taxpayer dollars — to pay for political ads,” Schumer said. “This is illegal, corrupt, and undemocratic — and now he’s following with another illegal act by directing his super PAC to pick up the tab for his propaganda. Donald Trump should not be able to get away with this gross waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars for his ridiculous propaganda ads. There must be an immediate investigation.”

The Schumer moves are mostly messaging signals, as it’s unclear whether the FEC will be able to investigate Trump. There are currently only two seated commissioners — both are Democratic appointees — with four vacant spots.

A spokesperson for the FEC declined to comment, as FEC complaints are confidential until they are resolved or closed.

articles.title: Abbott not joining Trump at San Antonio campaign stop
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) will not appear alongside President Trump at an upcoming political rally in San Antonio as the Republican incumbent fights for reelection less than a month out from November’s midterms. Trump is traveling to Texas Wednesday to stump for the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton (R), who is locked in a…
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) will not appear alongside President Trump at an upcoming political rally in San Antonio as the Republican incumbent fights for reelection less than a month out from November’s midterms.

Trump is traveling to Texas Wednesday to stump for the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton (R), who is locked in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico for a seat in the Senate. GOP House candidate Carlos De La Cruz, who’s running in a congressional district that includes parts of San Antonio, is also slated to attend.

Abbott’s campaign confirmed the governor’s plans to skip this event and directed The Hill back to his response to a reporter’s question at a Monday roundtable event with law enforcement in Houston.

“Because of the schedule that I run, where I go to multiple cities a day doing events like this, I already have events like this scheduled that day and I will not be able to make it,” Abbott said.

The governor praised the president’s ability to drum up “excitement among the base.”

“He does a good job of getting the base organized and turning out,” he added.

The Wednesday event will mark the president’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, a signal of the state’s importance in the GOP’s efforts to maintain control of Congress this fall.

Several Republican candidates in battleground states this election cycle have sought to distance themselves from the president amid concerns about rising living costs and the ongoing U.S. military operations against Iran.

Last month, Abbott praised the Trump administration’s illegal immigration crackdown during a speech at the GOP’s midterm convention in mid-September, which Trump and Vice President Vance also attended.

“I want you to know this much: We are very proud to have President Donald J. Trump here in Dallas, Texas,” Abbott told the crowd.

The governor was also asked during Monday’s roundtable about polling data that showed his Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa gaining ground in the state’s competitive gubernatorial race.

In a New York Times/Siena University poll conducted last month, the Democratic candidate posted a four-point lead on the incumbent Republican. A Fox News poll from the same time period showed Abbott with a five-point lead among registered voters.

“Listen, one thing I have is internal data, and I feel very comfortable about where I am,” Abbott replied.

articles.title: Maryland governor, White House spar over $3.7B submarine investment event
articles.summary: The White House and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) sparred on Tuesday over an event announcing a $3.7 billion investment from the defense contractor Anduril in a Baltimore shipyard to manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines. “We have been working with them for over a year to bring them on board, and we’re excited about what…
articles.body:
The White House and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) sparred on Tuesday over an event announcing a $3.7 billion investment from the defense contractor Anduril in a Baltimore shipyard to manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines.

“We have been working with them for over a year to bring them on board, and we’re excited about what it’s going to mean to the area,” Moore told reporters. “But if the president of the United States wants to bring the circus into town and tell me that I’m not allowed to speak to the fact that we were the ones to help bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to the work of the people of Maryland.

The White House accused Moore earlier on Tuesday of “throwing a tantrum” over the event announcing an investment in a Baltimore shipyard.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“President Trump is willing to work with anyone to revitalize our manufacturing sector, which is why the White House graciously invited Governor Moore to attend today’s event as a guest,” a White House official told The Hill ahead of the event.

“It’s unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion-dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over an announcement that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump,” they added.

A source familiar said earlier on Tuesday that Trump had “ blocked ” Moore from speaking at the event, at which Trump is set to give remarks.

“Governor Moore has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them,” a spokesperson for the governor said.

“The governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state,” they continued.

Moore was not the only Democrat from the state planning to miss Tuesday’s event. A source familiar told The Hill’s sister network NewsNation that Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is unable to attend the event due “prior engagements.”

Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) said in an interview with CNN from North Carolina on Tuesday that Trump should not get credit for the project.

“Absolutely not,” Alsobrooks said, adding, “Baltimore is strong on its face.”

Moore, who has been floated as a potential Democratic 2028 presidential contender , has sparred with the president in the past.

Anduril is investing in a new shipyard in Sparrows Point, Baltimore, where it will manufacture parts for Virginia-class submarines.

A senior administration official told reporters during a call Tuesday that $2.9 billion for the facility will come from the Pentagon and the Trump administration expects the funding to fit into the regular budget process.

Moore celebrated the project in a statement Tuesday.

“This massive new project will deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in over a decade — driving billions of dollars in economic activity that will boost Maryland families not just in Baltimore County, but throughout the state,” he wrote.

“With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs,” the governor added.
