articles.title: Newsom calls for 25th Amendment after Trump’s remarks on California
articles.summary: President Trump is stoking outrage among California Democrats and at least one House GOP candidate after he suggested at a midterm rally that he would allow Iran to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) led the charge, telling The Hill on Tuesday that Trump is “mentally ill.” “TIME FOR…
articles.body:
President Trump is stoking outrage among California Democrats and at least one House GOP candidate after he suggested at a midterm rally that he would allow Iran to “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) led the charge, telling The Hill on Tuesday that Trump is “mentally ill.”

“TIME FOR THE 25TH!” the governor said in a statement.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The sentiment follows a social media post from Newsom on Monday where he called Trump “deranged and dangerous.”

Newsom is widely seen as a prospective presidential contender for Democrats in 2028.

“Gavin Newscum is the worst governor in America, and he also may be the dumbest,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in response to the remarks.

Newsom was far from the only California politician lashing out at Trump, however.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) said Trump’s remarks are “dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) told Trump in his own statement to “keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

Meanwhile, Republican Jim Desmond, who is running for a San Diego-area House district, said he “vehemently” disagrees with the president.

“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage,” Desmond wrote on social media.

The president’s statement risks firing up Democrats ahead of the midterms as Republicans struggle to galvanize their own base.

“While the president’s statement may get laughs in Nebraska, in California it highlights why our state’s voters passionately dislike Trump,” said Matthew Klink, a California-based Republican strategist.

“Last night, apparently, the feeling became mutual,” he added.

The White House has vehemently pushed back against what it has called an unfair characterization of Trump’s remarks.

Steven Cheung, the White House’s communications director, said on social media that the “media freakout” over the comments “is not rooted in reality.”

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” Cheung wrote on social platform X.

But even some Trump allies didn’t see it that way.

“While it’s clear the president was joking, it’s not helpful to have these comments out there with a month to go,” said one former Trump campaign aide who is involved in the midterm efforts. “This isn’t his first time at the movie and he knows better. He knows when something is said even in jest, it’s a distraction for us.”

“It basically means that instead of focusing on Democrats, we’re addressing something he said,” the former aide said.

Democrats, meanwhile, were pleased to see California lawmakers like Newsom call out Trump on his comments.

“Good for Gavin, as he should,” said Democratic strategist Joel Payne. “Few people in modern American history have tried to turn the country against each other or use the bully pulpit of the presidency to turn people against each other more than Donald Trump.”

“Wishing harm on his own constituents that he is accountable to is as close to unforgivable as you could imagine for a public official and there will be little more than a peep from Republicans to call him out about it,” Payne added.

Garry South, a Democratic strategist based in California and a former adviser to Newsom, said the California governor was “right on” to call out Trump for “suggesting a foreign adversary target cities in his state.”

“Los Angeles is home to the largest expatriate Iranian community outside of Iran, not that ignoramus Trump probably knows that, but it makes it doubly egregious to put an Iranian target on Southern California,” South said.

Trump’s remarks are having a particular impact in Desmond’s race for California’s 48th Congressional District, which is one of the last few competitive races left in the state.

“He goes to Nebraska last night to rally the base, but the storyline of it will be Republican candidates in difficult races needing to once again distance themselves from the president,” said Rob Stutzman, a veteran California Republican strategist.

However, one Republican operative argued that the situation could help candidates like Desmond who were already seeking to put distance between themselves and the president in the blue state.

“Democrats have spent this entire race trying to convince voters that Jim Desmond would be simply a rubber stamp for President Trump,” the GOP operative said. “His statement yesterday is a pretty clear cut against that argument.”

Trump’s comment about the two Southern California cities was not the only controversial remark he made on the campaign trail Monday.

Trump used an anti-trans slur to refer to South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews in a Truth Social post while en route to last night’s rally in Nebraska.

“One of the biggest problems Republicans are facing is that the president of their party is unhinged,” Stutzman said. “He is being extremely counterproductive on the road to Republican political objectives.”

articles.title: 2028 Democratic contenders set to meet at post-midterm conference on party’s future
articles.summary: Potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders are expected to meet at the party’s post-midterm conference next month, with a focus on how to navigate through the next election and beyond. The conference, titled “What’s Next,” will be held Nov. 12-14 in Denver. It is not an official Democratic Party event, and instead will be presented by…
articles.body:
Potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders are expected to meet at the party’s post-midterm conference next month, with a focus on how to navigate through the next election and beyond.

The conference, titled “What’s Next,” will be held Nov. 12-14 in Denver. It is not an official Democratic Party event, and instead will be presented by Majority Democrats and sponsored by MD PAC.

“‘What’s Next’ is the defining convening of the post-election season, bringing together the people who will write the party’s next chapter,” the event’s description stated. “… Together, we’ll absorb what happened in 2026 and chart where the party goes next.”

The event page named 33 people who will “write the party’s next chapter” and attend the event. Names included former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former U.S. Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D), Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), Reps. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.) and Sarah McBride (D-Del.), Sens. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Democratic strategists David Axelrod and Lis Smith.

“More will be announced as the program comes together,” the conference website stated.

The conference looks to open up debate between “competing visions of the party’s future, and conversations with leading strategists, opinion leaders and candidates.” It will also allow partner organizations to discuss ideas and allow activists and other staffers to organize “opportunities” for the party.

Majority Democrats used the state where the conference will be located as a testament to the party’s 20-year goal to shift Colorado from red to purple to blue, “not by accident, but by investing in people and institutions, building a coalition and then delivering.”

The Democratic Party, which aims to reclaim one or both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections, is also looking to retake the White House following former Vice President Kamala Harris’s loss to President Trump in 2024.

Democrats that year faced growing unpopularity between rising costs and inflation, and growing unpopularity over the U.S.’s support for Israel in its war in Gaza. Paul Rivera, the author of the Democratic National Committee’s 2024 election “autopsy,” told Axios in August that the war hurt Harris politically.

The party has seen major gains this year from candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) winning against longtime Democratic incumbents.

articles.title: Plague cases still occur in the US: Here’s where
articles.summary: Earlier this year, a woman in New Mexico died of the plague, officials said.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) — While U.S. officials have said they are monitoring reports of a possible plague outbreak in Russia , they have cautioned that it isn’t a “cause for alarm.” Still, worries have grown over the nearly always fatal condition.

Person-to-person spread of the plague hasn’t been seen in more than 100 years in the U.S. However, Arizona reported a pneumonic plague-related death last year, and a New Mexico woman died from plague this year.

Between 2000 and 2023, between zero and 17 cases of human plague were reported in the U.S. each year, according to the most recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Fifteen of the 122 cases confirmed during that time period were fatal, the data shows.

When cases do occur in the U.S., they’re primarily in the West, with most reported in New Mexico and Arizona. Cases have also appeared near southern Oregon, far western Nevada, and California.

Last year, Oregon saw its first case of the bubonic plague since 2015 . Plague cases were also reported in California and New Mexico in 2025.

An Arizona resident fully recovered after being diagnosed with plague earlier this year. There have only been two cases of plague in the U.S. this year, CDC data shows.

Generally speaking, plague is brought on by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, with humans and mammals being affected. Cases in the U.S. are, most often, bubonic, which was the most common during Europe’s Black Death .

Bubonic plague is caused by the bites of fleas found on rodents. It can cause symptoms like a sudden high fever; chills; headaches; pain in the abdomen, arms, and legs; and large, swollen lymph nodes that can leak pus.

A case confirmed in Oregon in 2024 — the state’s first since 2015 — was believed to have been caused by a pet cat . Both the cat and its human owner were provided the necessary treatment, according to officials.

There are two other forms of plague: septicemic and pneumonic.

Septicemic plague has similar symptoms to bubonic plague, including fever, chills, extreme weakness, pain in the abdomen, shock, and the possibility of bleeding into the skin and other organs, the CDC explains . This form of plague can develop from untreated bubonic plague as well as from the handling of infected animals.

Should a person with bubonic or septicemic plague go without treatment, and the bacteria reach their lungs, they can develop pneumonic plague. The plague case reported in Russia is believed to be pneumonic.

Humans can also get pneumonic plague from breathing in “droplets coughed out by another person or animal with pneumonic plague,” according to the CDC. Like other forms of plague, symptoms can include a fever, headache, weakness, and pneumonia, with the latter developing “rapidly.”

While bubonic and septicemic plague may take a few days to set in, the incubation period for pneumonic plague may be just over a day, the CDC reports. It’s the only form that can be spread person-to-person, and it is considered the most serious form of the disease.

Roughly 90% of plague patients survive with quick treatment, regardless of which type they have contracted. Untreated, “plague is nearly always fatal,” the Cleveland Clinic said.

To avoid getting the plague, it’s recommended that you take steps to avoid flea bites. That includes wearing bug spray with DEET and clearing up spaces outside where flea-loving wild animals may live. It’s also important to speak with your veterinarian about preventing fleas on your pets. Your pets should also not be allowed to roam outdoors freely if you live in an area prone to the plague.

articles.title: Pappas leads Sununu by 7 points in New Hampshire Senate race: Poll
articles.summary: New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is leading in the state’s open U.S. Senate race against Republican nominee John E. Sununu, according to new polling released Tuesday. The New Hampshire Institute of Politics (NHIP) survey, commissioned by AARP, found the Democrat holds a 7-point advantage over his Republican opponent among likely voters in the state.…
articles.body:
New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas (D) is leading in the state’s open U.S. Senate race against Republican nominee John E. Sununu , according to new polling released Tuesday.

The New Hampshire Institute of Politics (NHIP) survey , commissioned by AARP, found the Democrat holds a 7-point advantage over his Republican opponent among likely voters in the state.

The poll, which included an oversample of people aged 50 years or older, showed Pappas had a slimmer, one-point advantage among this voting demographic.

AARP’s New Hampshire state director, Christina FitzPatrick, emphasized the importance of gaining the support of older voters in this race, saying the “candidates must address their priorities.”

“With affordability a top concern for New Hampshire residents this year, candidates should tell voters how they will protect and strengthen Social Security and ensure that everyone is able to age with dignity and purpose,” FitzPatrick said in a statement.

The candidates are competing in the November race for the open seat to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Pappas has represented the Granite State in the House since 2019, and he has been part of the Problem Solvers Caucus since 2023.

Sununu served in both chambers of Congress for over a decade before he lost his Senate seat to Shaheen in 2008. He is related to former New Hampshire Govs. John H. Sununu and Chris Sununu.

Both candidates handily won their primary races last month to advance to the November election. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, shifted its rating in this race from “lean D” to a “toss up” following the September election.

The state has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate in over a decade, although the GOP has controlled the state’s governor mansion since 2017.

The Democratic candidate has maintained a slight lead ahead of Sununu in recent polling. Pappas posted a 5-point advantage in a New York Times/Siena University poll and an 8-point advantage in a University of New Hampshire survey last month.

The AARP/NHIP survey was conducted among 1,042 likely New Hampshire voters from Sept. 28 to 29 with a margin of error of approximately 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Lawyers urge watchdogs to examine Reflecting Pool case against ex-Olympian
articles.summary: Lawyers for a former U.S. Olympian cleared of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are asking federal watchdogs to investigate how the Justice Department built a felony case against him before prosecutors concluded he was not responsible. Attorneys for David Hearn on Tuesday sent a letter to the inspectors general at the DOJ and Interior…
articles.body:
Lawyers for a former U.S. Olympian cleared of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool are asking federal watchdogs to investigate how the Justice Department built a felony case against him before prosecutors concluded he was not responsible.

Attorneys for David Hearn on Tuesday sent a letter to the inspectors general at the DOJ and Interior Department asking the watchdogs to look into what they describe as a flawed investigation and prosecution, alleging officials overlooked critical evidence and rushed to charge Hearn amid pressure from President Trump.

The complaint comes days D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Eldeman permanently dismissed the case against the former Olympian, describing it as a “lightning-fast indictment process” and barred the DOJ from trying to charge him again in the future.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Edelman found that there was a “unique possibility” that U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office would likely attempt to revive the case against him due to “political pressure” from Trump to prosecute suspected vandals.

“In light of these findings and the government’s own admissions, a critical purpose of the requested investigations is to collect the facts — through witness interviews and the collection and analysis of electronic media and documents — necessary to hold accountable the individuals and groups who failed Mr. Hearn, the criminal justice system, and the public,” Hearn’s lawyers wrote in their letter.

Hearn, 67, had been charged with felony property destruction in June after he was arrested and accused of damaging the Reflecting Pool’s newly installed liner.

Pirro moved to drop the charge weeks later after evidence from the Interior Department showed Hearn did not cause the damage, and that the issue stemmed from problems with the pool’s multi-million dollar renovation and accelerated efforts to complete the project ahead of America’s 250th birthday celebrations.

Hearn’s attorneys now argue that evidence cleaning him was available to the government well before prosecutors abandoned the case.

“The record reflects an indictment obtained through unusual haste and a prosecution shaped from the outset by political pressure and built on an inadequate investigation,” his lawyers wrote.

articles.title: Cook Political Report moves three Senate races in Democrats’ favor
articles.summary: The Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, is shifting its odds for Senate races in Kansas, North Carolina and New Hampshire toward Democrats. The changes show how unfavorable the political environment continues to be for Republican candidates amid the war in Iran and the state of the economy. These races being more competitive could spell…
articles.body:
The Cook Political Report, an election handicapper, is shifting its odds for Senate races in Kansas, North Carolina and New Hampshire toward Democrats.

The changes show how unfavorable the political environment continues to be for Republican candidates amid the war in Iran and the state of the economy.

These races being more competitive could spell optimism for Democrats in their chances to retake the Senate majority.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“At this point, the question isn’t whether Democrats will gain seats, but how many,” said Jessica Taylor, Senate and governors editor at Cook. “As such, we are revising our estimate of potential pickups to two to six seats for Democrats — squarely within the range of the four seats they need to net for a majority.”

The Kansas race, once thought reliably red, has picked up steam in recent weeks. Adam Hamilton, a pastor and founder of the largest United Methodist church in the country, is running as a moderate Democrat, hoping to unseat Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas).

Hamilton has attacked Marshall over his connection to Trump and the unpopular war in Iran, while Marshall has aimed to paint Hamilton as “woke,” claiming he supports a socially liberal approach to Christian theology.

Polls show Hamilton and Marshall neck and neck, significant for a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century.

National Republicans have noticed: They’re pulling money out of North Carolina and putting it in Kansas to back Marshall.

North Carolina also seems more favorable to Democrats than ever. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, has been polling significantly ahead of Republican political operative Michael Whatley for much of the summer . Both parties have lessened their investment in that state in recent days, a sign that its battleground status is waning.

The race rating change for New Hampshire is notable, as Cook moved it to “toss-up” in Republicans’ favor last month . Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is running for the seat being vacated by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), while former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican who served one term in the chamber 18 years ago, is looking for a comeback.

But while Sununu hails from a prominent political family and Pappas is lesser known, the Granite State is looking friendly to Democrats again. Two polls at the tail end of September, one from AARP and one from a Republican polling group, both had Pappas up by 7.

articles.title: Johnson predicts a Democratic majority will impeach Trump immediately
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is predicting that Democrats will waste no time impeaching President Trump if they win control of the lower chamber in the midterm elections. “It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day — first or second day,” Johnson said Tuesday in an interview with Scott Jennings, a pro-Trump pundit. “Remember, they’ve already…
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is predicting that Democrats will waste no time impeaching President Trump if they win control of the lower chamber in the midterm elections.

“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day — first or second day,” Johnson said Tuesday in an interview with Scott Jennings, a pro-Trump pundit. “Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress. And they’re raring to go.”

Johnson’s remarks are both a warning to Republicans and a campaign message designed to get GOP voters to the polls in November’s elections, when Democrats are now favored , by many handicappers, to win the House majority.

Polls indicate that Trump’s policies are widely unpopular, even among many Republicans, but a much smaller number support his removal from office. Many liberals want him ousted, but many other Democrats fear that talk of impeachment will only energize GOP voters who might otherwise sit the midterms out.

Those dynamics have created a minefield for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his leadership team, who are fighting to keep the party focused on the volatile economy even as liberals on and off of Capitol Hill are ramping up their calls to remove Trump from office.

Jeffries, who is in line to become Speaker if the House changes hands, has sought to balance those competing pressures by keeping all options open while committing to none.

“We haven’t ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to us to hold people accountable, and we haven’t ruled anything in,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington last month, as the House was leaving town for the long election recess. “That’s been our position. That will remain our position.”

Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), the chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, went a step further to defuse the impeachment talk, dismissing the idea as a Republican scare-tactic.

“This is something, oftentimes, I think the right-wing media wants us to talk about,” Aguilar said in late September. “But it’s not anything that is top of the agenda for House Democrats.”

Democrats were forced to confront the impeachment question head on last month, when Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) forced a vote on impeachment articles related to the deaths of civilians at the hands of federal immigration enforcement officers. The resolution was supported by 147 Democrats — nearly 70 percent of the caucus — but Jeffries, Aguilar and other party leaders distanced themselves from the effort by voting “present.”

Green will be gone next year, a casualty of Trump’s mid-district redistricting push. But a number of incoming liberals want Democrats to fight harder against the administration, and they may take up the impeachment mantle where Green left off.

Johnson, for his part, maintains that all the talk of impeachment is largely irrelevant because Republicans, he says, will keep control of the House next year.

“This is not going to happen,” he told Jennings. “Let’s just paint this alternative world, OK. Cause I’m convinced, Scott, we can hold this majority.”

articles.title: White House, DOJ pushed FBI to investigate protesters, violating rights: Whistleblower
articles.summary: A new whistleblower complaint accuses the White House as well as top leadership at the Justice Department and the FBI of directing agents to open investigations into Los Angeles protestors, violating the Constitution and bureau policy by targeting them for First Amendment activity. The complaint from former FBI intelligence analyst Jill Fields relays that she…
articles.body:
A new whistleblower complaint accuses the White House as well as top leadership at the Justice Department and the FBI of directing agents to open investigations into Los Angeles protestors, violating the Constitution and bureau policy by targeting them for First Amendment activity.

The complaint from former FBI intelligence analyst Jill Fields relays that she was reassigned from the cartels squad in the Los Angeles Field Office amid widespread protests last year responding to Trump administration immigration enforcement.

Fields’ disclosure was released by Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), who demanded a response from FBI Director Kash Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche. He said the complaint shows both agencies were willing to start investigations “at the behest of the White House and Trump loyalists, over the objection of senior staff, and in contravention of agency policy and the Constitution.”

The report describes two incidents in which either the White House or DOJ officials pressured FBI staff to open investigations into protestors.

In the first, which occurred in February 2025, Fields said she was told to start an investigation after frustrations over a video showing protestors using megaphones to warn residents about the presence of immigration officers was “communicated down from the White House to Kash Patel.”

In another instance, the former No. 2 at the Justice Department, Emil Bove, directed FBI staff to open an investigation into protestors demonstrating outside federal buildings in Los Angeles.

The report noted that investigations against protestors solely for First Amendment activity are explicitly illegal and contrary to FBI policy.

In the first incident, protestors using megaphones in Alhambra, Calif., near Los Angeles were telling those facing arrest about their rights.

Fields was told that “the President viewed the footage on social media and instructed FBI Director Kash Patel to have the Los Angeles Field Office open an investigation into the protesters.”

Another FBI figure, whose name is redacted in the report, told Fields that in a meeting with Patel, “participants had been informed that the President had viewed video footage of the Alhambra protesters, he was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested.”

The report states that a preliminary review of the FBI found that “video recording, use of a megaphone, and verbal objection—were constitutionally protected under the First Amendment and never crossed the line into impeding arrest or being a threat.”

In the second incident, the report cites Bove as being behind another request for an investigation into protestors who were staging their activities near federal buildings in Los Angeles.

“Ms. Fields knew from her training and experience that it was extraordinarily unusual for the DOJ or an Acting Deputy Attorney General to directly contact an [assistant director in charge] regarding the opening of an FBI investigative matter,” the report states.

“Ms. Fields also knew based on her experience that the FBI does not open assessments or investigations based on First Amendment protected activity, unless there were actual or potential national security threats or federal criminal activity, or vulnerability to such threats, none of which had been identified here.”

The report says the request came amid other odd practices. Supervisors encouraged Fields and others to not put things in writing and she noticed many directives and subsequent discussions were conducted in face-to-face meetings rather than over email.

She also questioned why she was being moved from her assignment monitoring cartels to take on oversight of investigations into protestors.

“Los Angeles is a major transshipment hub for drug trafficking and Ms. Fields questioned the directive’s operational logic, as agents were pulled off active cartel cases to satisfy what her supervisor described as ‘optics’ designed to ‘make a show for the president,’” the report states.

Padilla in his letter asked a series of questions about the investigations, noting both Patel and Blanche had promised not to pursue political investigations.

“Throughout your appearances before the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, you promised that cases would be based only on the facts and the law, free from political interference. But the Disclosure paints a starkly different picture and raises serious questions about whether other similar investigations have been initiated under your tenures,” he wrote.

“Such allegations raise grave concerns about the rule of law under your leadership, the diversion of resources from ongoing criminal investigations, and the testimony that you provided under oath to Congress.”

The DOJ and the FBI in a joint statement dismissed the report as a politically motivated attack.

“Under President Trump, the Department of Justice will continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law. The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law. Violence is not protected by the First Amendment. Politically motivated attacks will not deter us from doing our job,” the statement said.

Fields resigned from her job at the FBI after she was reassigned.

“Ms. Fields believes this reassignment constituted retaliation for her protected disclosures. No comparable action had been taken against her until after she objected to the protest-related investigations and reported those concerns outside her chain of command,” the report states.

articles.title: Wes Moore dodges commitment to full second term if reelected: Report
articles.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) did not give a clear answer during a Tuesday debate on if he would serve his full term if he were to be reelected in November, according to multiple reports. The Baltimore Banner reported that the governor dodged a question on whether he would see through the entire duration of…
articles.body:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) did not give a clear answer during a Tuesday debate on if he would serve his full term if he were to be reelected in November, according to multiple reports.

The Baltimore Banner reported that the governor dodged a question on whether he would see through the entire duration of a second term should he beat Republican Dan Cox this fall. The line of questioning came as some look to Moore as a promising Democratic contender for the 2028 presidential race.

When asked about staying in his role for another four years, the governor replied, “Being the governor of Maryland has been the honor of a lifetime,” the Banner reported.

“And I would not be running for reelection if I was not committed to the people of Maryland,” he added.

Moore was then pushed for a definitive answer, to which he said, “I gave the answer. I am committed to the people of Maryland. That’s why I am running for reelection.”

The Maryland governor, first elected in 2022, has denied he plans to pursue the presidency in 2028, telling NBC News last year that “I’m not running for president.” He also asserted at the time that, should he reclaim the gubernatorial seat, “I’ll be serving a full term”

In September 2025, Moore said he was “living the dream” as governor after announcing his reelection bid. The Democrat has been a frequent critic of President Trump throughout his tenure in Maryland’s highest office.

“I’m excited about running for reelection. And, you know, I’m literally a person who was raised by an immigrant, single mom, who had handcuffs on my wrist when I was 11 years old, who’s now serving as the 63rd governor of my state and the first Black governor in the history of the state of Maryland,” Moore told CNN’s Erin Burnett on “OutFront” at the time.

“I am — I am living the dream right now, and our state is doing well,” he added. “And I’m excited to go back in front of the people of my state.”

Moore appears safe in his seat, as the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates his race as solidly Democratic less than a month before Election Day.
